data.title: Goldman Sachs 2027 Macro Outlook: Precious Metals Seem to Be Back to 2022
data.description:
This week's recent bloodbath in non-ferrous and precious metals is reminiscent of the fleeting beauty of a thousand miles in a single day. Interest rate hikes, AI-driven regulatory clearing under the blue wave, and deleveraging have made for a truly turbulent year-end market. Goldman Sachs' 2027 macroeconomic outlook has just been released, so let's see how they view precious metals.

■ For precious metals, 2027 is increasingly resembling 2022: rising Fed policy rates are suppressing private investor demand, but structural gold purchases by central banks are providing solid support for gold prices. Therefore, we believe there are short-term downside risks and increased volatility during the Fed's continued rate hikes, but with continued central bank gold purchases, we still expect gold prices to slowly climb to $4,650/ounce by the end of 2027. Once the Fed begins cutting interest rates, we expect demand for Western ETFs to rebound, pushing gold prices even stronger to $5,600/oz by the end of 2028. The baseline scenario carries significant upside risk if macroeconomic policies offset the return of demand. ■ The same 2022 scenario should favor gold over silver. Interest rate hikes suppress private investment demand for both metals, but only gold benefits from structural buying by central banks. Therefore, we expect gold to outperform silver in 2027 unless another silver liquidity squeeze occurs—which we believe is unsustainable given the Fed's rate hike cycle and pressure on silver ETF demand. ■ For platinum and palladium, continued uncertainty surrounding US tariffs should keep supply fragmented and volatility high, but does not necessarily mean higher prices in 2027. Interest rate hikes should suppress investment demand—especially for platinum, which accounts for a larger share of investment than palladium, while rising electric vehicle penetration remains a structural headwind for automotive demand. Platinum faces greater pressure as European fleets, which have a higher proportion of diesel vehicles, shift to electric vehicles; while palladium's demand decline in automotive catalysts should be more gradual due to the rising share of hybrid vehicles and a slower electrification transition in the US market, which has a higher proportion of gasoline vehicles. ■ In this 2027 outlook, we discuss our views on precious metals, key risks, and implications for investors in a Q&A format: we cover the upside and downside risks to our gold forecast, why gold failed to hedge against the 2026 Strait of Hormuz supply shock, how opportunities vary depending on investor horizons, why we expect central bank gold purchases to remain structural, and the risks of the People's Bank of China's gold purchases and potential official selling. We then turn to why we expect gold to outperform silver during the Fed's rate hike cycle, and why continued supply disruptions will cause platinum and palladium prices to fluctuate but not necessarily drive prices higher.

I. Gold: Structural Central Bank Support Amid Cyclical Interest Rate Headwinds

Question 1: What are your gold price forecasts for 2027 and beyond?

We maintain a constructive view on gold in the long term, based on structurally strong central bank gold purchases (including by the People's Bank of China), but given the Fed's hawkish outlook, we believe the short-term environment is more challenging.

Our economists expect a third 25 basis point rate hike in March 2027, following the anticipated second rate hike in December 2026, suppressing demand for interest rate-sensitive Western ETFs.

Nevertheless, we expect continued central bank gold purchases to push gold prices to $4,650 by the end of 2027, a 19% increase from the spot price and a 13% increase from the October average (Figures 1 & 2).

The Fed's recent hawkish shift and rising policy rates should also dampen investors' "currency devaluation concerns."

Therefore, we assume that macroeconomic policy hedging demand for gold—reflected in call option demand—will revert to its historical average (Figure 3). We expect private investor demand (reflected through demand for interest rate-sensitive Western ETFs) to eventually rebound after four 25-basis-point rate cuts between November 2027 and September 2028, bringing the federal funds rate down to a terminal rate of 3.25%–3.5%, thereby removing interest rate constraints on gold prices and supporting a rise to $5,600/oz by the end of 2028 (Figure 1). Figure 1: We forecast gold to be at $4,650/oz by the end of 2027 and $5,600/oz by the end of 2028. Figure 2: We maintain our long-term constructive view on strong structural central bank demand – which drives most of our projected price upside to the end of 2027. Starting from an October average of $4,100/oz, we believe the recent price weakness is primarily driven by speculative positioning and may therefore prove temporary.

Figure 3: We expect macroeconomic policy hedging demand for gold—reflected in call option demand and potentially a key amplifier of the 2025/early 2026 rally—to further retreat to historical levels.

We believe the 2027 landscape will resemble 2022 (Figure 4): central banks will provide strong structural buying, but higher federal funds rates will suppress investor positioning, resulting in a more moderate net increase in gold prices.

Figure 4: The current situation is similar to 2022: Central banks provide strong structural buying, but higher interest rates suppress investor positioning. **Question 2: What risks do you face in your gold forecast?** We believe a more hawkish Fed stance poses further downside risks in the short term. In a scenario with four rate hikes and higher terminal rates (Figure 6), we estimate gold prices to be $4,585/oz by the end of 2027 (red dashed line in Figure 5). Larger ETF selling could further depress prices. The significant increase in gold ETF holdings over the past three years reflects a normal upward trend driven by lower interest rates, investor wealth growth (captured by our interest rate-implied autoregressive ETF model), and the potential boost from recent depreciation trades. We expect two additional Fed rate hikes to eliminate the latter, but cannot clearly distinguish it from structural wealth trends. As a conservative lower bound, we therefore assume that all ETF holdings exceeding the level implied by interest rates alone will be reduced, implying an additional 300 tons of selling, with the gold price at $4,265/oz by the end of 2027 (grey dashed line in Figure 5, Figure 7). Figure 5: Higher terminal interest rates and ETF sell-offs pose downside risks to our baseline scenario (US$4,650/oz by the end of 2027). Figure 6: Our US economists project a rate hike in December 2026 and another in March 2027; further rate hikes and higher terminal interest rates pose downside risks to our gold price forecast. Figure 7: A more hawkish Fed could—in extreme scenarios—drive a reduction of 300 tons of gold ETF holdings.

There are also tactical downside risks surrounding our fair value forecast. Our forecast captures the slower-moving drivers of gold prices, namely demand from Western ETFs and central banks, but speculative positioning could temporarily deviate prices from fair value. COMEX speculative positioning is already at a low 45th percentile, and we expect it to rebound in the baseline scenario. That said, rising oil prices could trigger further systemic CTA selling, while a sharp pullback in equities (e.g., related to AI cycle uncertainty) could initially drag gold lower as margin calls and broader deleveraging force investors to raise cash (Figure 8).

Figure 8: Intraday, rising oil prices suppressed gold through systemic selling, while the sharp stock market pullback initially suppressed it through deleveraging. In the long term, if macroeconomic policy hedging demand returns after the Fed begins cutting rates, we believe there is significant upside potential beyond the baseline scenario. Perceived fiscal sustainability concerns in Western economies, potentially exacerbated by increased military spending and rising debt burdens in energy-importing countries, could revive this macroeconomic policy hedging demand if investors also begin to worry about how developed market central banks will respond. Once lower interest rates remove the ceiling on gold price increases, the potential resurgence of fiscal sustainability concerns could push gold prices significantly beyond our baseline scenario of $5,600/oz by the end of 2028. Question 3: Gold did not rise despite rising inflation during the 2026 Strait of Hormuz impact. Has gold's role as an inflation hedge or safe-haven asset changed? We believe not. We have long argued that gold is not a universally applicable stagflation hedge because the source of inflation is crucial. There are two distinct stagflation scenarios in which stock-bond portfolios typically underperform, and gold performs differently in each. The first scenario is characterized by growing market concerns about institutional credibility. When markets doubt central banks' willingness or ability to curb inflation, inflation can spike, causing both bonds and stocks to fall. The 1970s are a prime example: US fiscal expansion and the loss of Federal Reserve independence fueled runaway inflation, and gold surged as investors sought a store of value outside the system. The second scenario involves supply disruptions that simultaneously weaken growth and drive up prices, such as in 2022 when Russia (which then supplied 40% of Europe's gas) cut supply. Commodities—as disrupted inputs—are among the few assets with positive real returns. As in 2022, gold typically underperforms initially in supply disruption events. Supply-driven inflation increases the risk of monetary policy tightening, rising yields increase the opportunity cost of holding gold and suppress ETF demand, while potential stock market pullbacks trigger margin-related liquidations. The 2026 Strait of Hormuz shock falls into the second scenario, as the inflationary shock originates from disrupted commodity supplies. Question 4: What advice do you have for investors? ■ The next 3-6 months may remain challenging for CTAs and macro hedge funds: rising federal funds rates in our baseline scenario, high uncertainty in energy prices, volatility from inflation and labor market data, and strict drawdown limits all make maintaining long positions difficult. Higher oil prices could add pressure through systemic selling, while a sharp stock market pullback could initially drag gold lower as margin calls and broader deleveraging force investors to raise cash. ■ However, for long-term investors seeking exposure to rising central bank demand and/or tail risks in macroeconomic policy (i.e., gold as a "depreciation" hedge), the current gold price pullback may offer a more attractive entry point. Structural central bank demand remains supportive, and private wealth and other long-term investors may value gold as insurance against fiscal sustainability risks in developed markets, even if these risks are not realized in our baseline scenario.

Question 5: Central bank demand is a key pillar of your gold outlook. Why do you believe this demand is structural and expect continued gold purchases?

Our view of strong structural central bank demand drives most of our projected price upside through the end of 2027 (60 tonnes per month from 2026–2028, compared to an average of 17 tonnes per month before 2022).

Although the seasonally adjusted 3-month moving average fell to 51 tonnes per month in September from 85 tonnes per month in August, we expect gold purchases to have resumed as prices subsequently stabilized, thus placing greater emphasis on the previously stronger months (Figure 9). Figure 9: Our Goldman Sachs immediate forecast for central bank gold purchases fell to the seasonally adjusted 3-month baseline of 51 tonnes per month in September, down from 85 tonnes per month in August (compared to the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes per month). Since the freezing of Russian reserves in 2022, central banks—especially emerging market central banks—have accelerated their gold purchases by approximately five times. We view this as a structural shift in reserve management behavior and do not expect it to reverse in the short term. Our baseline scenario assumes that the current cumulative trend in the official sector continues for another three years. Our rationale is that emerging market central banks' gold allocations remain significantly lower than their developed market counterparts, and the motivation to diversify away from G7 reserve currencies (including geopolitical and financial risks) may still exist. For example, we estimate that China—the largest buyer—holds approximately 11.8% of its reserves in gold, compared to approximately 80% for the US, Germany, France, and Italy (Figure 11). The global average is over 20%, which we consider a reasonable medium-term target for large emerging market central banks, based on historical precedent, current allocations, and our communications with emerging market central bank reserve managers. For example, Russia increased its gold holdings from 8% to 20% between 2014 and 2020 and repatriated its gold reserves before sanctions. If the largest official buyer—China—targets a 20% allocation and maintains an average purchase pace of approximately 20 tonnes per month (consistent with its 12-month moving average) (Figure 10), we estimate it would take approximately three years to reach a 20% gold holding. Our estimates also take into account the potential for continued global central bank gold purchases (60 tonnes/month) to push up gold prices over time—thus increasing the nominal value of existing holdings and helping to reach allocation targets more quickly (see Appendix for details). A recent World Gold Council survey supports our view: of the 76 central banks surveyed between February and May 2026, a record 45% expect to increase their own gold reserves in the next 12 months—the highest percentage since the survey began in 2018—while approximately 90% expect global reserves to rise, with the remainder expecting holdings to remain largely stable. Figure 10: China was the largest identifiable buyer in September, purchasing 20 tonnes of gold. Figure 11: China's estimated 11.8% gold allocation leaves ample room to reach a reasonable 20% target. Question 6: Will China's gold allocation eventually exceed your reasonable 20% target? Yes. We believe there is upside risk to China's 20% gold allocation target, as larger gold reserves could support the internationalization of the renminbi. The path for a currency to become a more important international currency generally involves three steps: increased use in third-party trade, increased role in international bond markets, and ultimately, its establishment in the reserves of other countries. While the first two steps are already underway, the final step is typically the harvest stage for any emerging reserve currency, as reserve managers seek to diversify from the existing reserve system while also considering the asset composition supporting the alternative currency. History suggests that gold can help complete this transition: as a reserve asset independent of any issuer's credit or political stance, gold can enhance confidence in an international currency. After World War II, substantial gold holdings helped support confidence that the US dollar had surpassed the British pound as the dominant reserve currency, reinforcing the notion that the currency was "as reliable as gold." Therefore, regardless of whether an emerging currency ultimately achieves dominant reserve status, gold accumulation can be part of a strategy, suggesting that China's desired gold allocation may eventually exceed 20%. Question 7: Reports indicate that the Turkish central bank has sold off a large amount of reserves since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict. Will central bank gold sales expand? We believe a broader central bank gold sell-off is unlikely—our immediate forecasts actually show a rebound in central bank gold purchases since May—and even the reported decline from Turkey may overstate the actual sell-off. Turkey's reserve reporting method is unusual because gold swaps can show a decline in reported gold reserves even if the gold is not directly sold, which may explain in part the 129-ton drop at the beginning of the Middle East conflict and its subsequent rapid rebound (Figure 12). Figure 12: Data from the Turkish Central Bank shows that gold reserves rebounded after a drop of 129 tons at the beginning of the Middle East conflict. More fundamentally, Turkey is an exception: as an emerging market central bank, it faces potential foreign exchange liquidity needs, and its unusually high allocation of over 60% of its foreign exchange reserves to gold makes gold (swaps) a more natural source of liquidity than most emerging market reserve managers (who typically hold well below 20%). Only a few countries share this characteristic: Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan also have unusually high gold allocations, while Russia and Venezuela face more specific restrictions on other reserve assets, similarly making gold a more natural source of liquidity. Therefore, we view these countries as more likely exceptions to gold swaps or sell-offs, rather than signals of a broader sell-off by emerging market central banks. We are skeptical of concerns that Gulf states might also sell off their gold reserves. The proportion of gold in the Gulf states' reserves is significantly lower. Gold accounts for approximately 4% of the UAE's reserves, 8% of Saudi Arabia's, 5% of Oman's, and about 24% of Qatar's, compared to over 60% of Turkey's foreign exchange reserves (Figure 13)—an unusually high proportion for an emerging market economy. Gulf economies typically peg to the US dollar, meaning that foreign exchange intervention is more likely to be carried out by selling US Treasury bonds rather than gold. The Gulf's reserve structure reduces the likelihood that its central banks would liquidate gold for foreign exchange management purposes. Figure 13: Turkey's proportion of gold in its foreign exchange reserves is significantly higher than that of the Gulf states. Question 8: Will developed market central banks holding large legacy gold reserves become sellers? We believe this risk is currently small. If anything, interest in gold and reserve security is expanding beyond emerging market central banks. Since 2022, developed market central banks have largely remained on the sidelines of the gold-buying spree, partly because they already hold substantial gold reserves for historical reasons, typically dispersed across domestic and international custodians, particularly the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, to manage jurisdictional, political, and physical risks. Concerns about geopolitical instability were one reason some European central banks moved some of their gold reserves to New York during the Cold War. However, feedback from developed market central banks suggests the discussion is increasingly shifting from whether to hold gold to where to store it: for example, France and the Netherlands have recently made repeated moves to move their gold reserves out of New York. This greater focus on reserve security indicates that developed market reserve managers are increasingly considering the tail risks that initially give gold its strategic value, reinforcing the rationale for holding rather than selling it.

II. Silver: The Run Ends, But the Fed Continues to Raise Rates

Question 9: Silver had an extraordinary start to the year, peaking above $120/oz with extreme price volatility. Do you expect a repeat in 2027?

Our baseline scenario is no. The silver rally in 2025/26 reflects an unusual combination of rising investor demand and tight liquidity in London, which we do not expect to be repeated during the Fed's rate hike cycle (Figure 14).

Figure 14: Silver peaked in early 2026 due to a clash between rising investor demand and tight liquidity in London. Speculation surrounding US trade policy—silver being included on the critical minerals list, and therefore theoretically eligible for tariffs even if exempted in April 2025—encouraged the pre-shipment of the metal to the US in 2025, drawing inventories away from London, which sets global benchmark prices. As London inventories dwindled, strong investor flows—supported by Fed rate cuts, silver chasing gold, and spillover effects from devaluation trades—absorbed an increasingly larger share of the remaining available metal, ultimately triggering a liquidity squeeze (Figure 15). While a weekly net demand of 1,000 tonnes of silver typically boosts prices by about 2%, we estimate that price sensitivity rises to about 7% during a run. As investor demand subsequently weakens and tensions ease, prices fall sharply. Figure 15: Tariff concerns draw silver to the US, draining London inventories; subsequent surge in investor demand absorbs the remaining silver, disproportionately impacting prices. We believe a repeat of the 2025/26 run in 2027 is unlikely: even if new tariff concerns again draw silver from London to the US, a Fed rate hike in early 2027 should suppress ETF demand, eliminating the second leg of the 2025/26 run. Once the Fed resumes its easing policies, surging ETF demand could push silver prices higher again, but another liquidity crunch in London could require renewed tariff concerns and a restart of US inventory accumulation. Question 10: Is the gold-silver ratio still worth watching? Will silver outperform gold again as the ratio returns to near the top of its historical range? No, we believe gold may outperform silver again in 2027, at least during the Fed's rate hike cycle. Like gold—investment demand is the primary driver of silver prices. Historically, private investment flows in the gold and silver markets have moved in tandem (Figure 16), keeping the gold-silver ratio within a wide range of 45-80 (Figure 17). Figure 16: Key Drivers of Silver and Gold – Private Investment Flows – Moving in Tandem… However, since 2022, gold has decoupled from its price, driven by a surge in central bank purchases, pushing up prices even without private investment inflows. Silver, lacking central bank buying, has lagged behind. Figure 17: ...The gold-silver price ratio remained within a wide range of 45-80 before gold decoupled due to central bank gold purchases in 2022. The 2025/26 London silver liquidity squeeze temporarily reversed this divergence, pushing silver prices sharply higher and the gold-silver ratio to the bottom of its historical range. As the squeeze subsided, the gold-silver ratio returned to the top of its range, but we do not believe this signals a return to silver outperforming. Fed rate hikes should suppress private investment demand for both metals, but gold has retained structural buying from central banks. Given that another silver liquidity squeeze during a rate hike cycle is unlikely (see Question 9), we expect gold to outperform silver again in 2027, at least until the Fed resumes its accommodative stance.

III. Platinum and Palladium: Still Segmented

Question 11: Platinum and palladium remain under the US Section 232 tariff investigation. What does this mean for the outlook?

We believe the main risks are continued supply segmentation and volatility stemming from ongoing uncertainty surrounding US tariffs (Figure 18), but we believe actual US tariffs on platinum and palladium are unlikely.

Figure 18: US Tariff Risks Since 2025 Drive Platinum and Palladium Supply Segmentation, Exacerbating Volatility and Run Risk

Platinum and palladium are key inputs, especially for the automotive industry, but global supply is unusually concentrated: Southern Africa accounts for approximately 82%/46% of platinum/palladium supply, and Russia accounts for another 11%/39%—creating a significant risk of disruption.

Reducing reliance on foreign supplies of key minerals and rebuilding domestic capacity appear to be increasingly important policy objectives for the United States. Theoretically, tariffs are one way to achieve this policy objective: making imported minerals more expensive, protecting domestic producers, and ultimately incentivizing investment in U.S. mines, smelters, and refineries. In practice, the supply response to platinum group metals is limited. Domestic U.S. mineral production is limited, expanding output is technically and geologically challenging, and new mines and refineries take years to be approved, built, and put into operation. Because tariffs change much faster than capacity building, the resulting policy uncertainty could undermine the long-term investment it is intended to encourage. However, tariff risks can still achieve national security objectives by attracting metal inventories to the U.S. without large-scale government purchases or immediately raising costs for downstream consumers. The result is reduced liquidity outside the U.S.—leading to price volatility—even if global inventories appear ample on paper. Question 12: Does continued supply disruption mean higher platinum and palladium prices in 2027? Not necessarily. Supply disruptions keep volatility risks high, but the demand landscape in 2027 is more complex. Fed rate hikes should suppress investment demand, particularly for platinum, which accounts for a larger share of investment than palladium. The electric vehicle transition should also continue to reduce demand for platinum group metals, although the impact may differ for the two metals. Platinum faces greater headwinds from European electric vehicles, but also gains more upside potential due to defense spending. Historically, Europe has had a higher proportion of diesel vehicles, making its fleet relatively more reliant on platinum. Therefore, the rising penetration rate of electric vehicles has a particularly significant impact on platinum demand. Our automotive analyst report states that in August 2026, sales of pure electric vehicles in Europe increased by 66% year-on-year, while implied sales of internal combustion engines decreased by 10% year-on-year. However, military vehicles remain highly dependent on diesel, making higher defense spending a potential offsetting factor. Palladium receives more support from hybrid vehicles and the slower US electric vehicle transition. Gasoline vehicles are more reliant on palladium, while hybrid vehicle growth supports palladium demand, as hybrid vehicles are primarily gasoline-powered. In the US, pure electric vehicle sales declined by 45% year-on-year in Q3 2026, while hybrid vehicle sales increased by 27% year-on-year. This suggests that demand for gasoline-powered catalysts may persist longer as the share of hybrid vehicles increases and the adoption of pure electric vehicles slows.

data.title: "Super Dollar" in 2027?
data.description:
Author: Zhang Yaqi Source: Wall Street News

The AI ​​boom is reshaping global capital flows, the dollar is hovering at high levels, but the fragile support structure makes the prospects of the super dollar uncertain.

... According to TrendFocus, Deutsche Bank significantly raised its 2027 US dollar forecast in its latest foreign exchange outlook report, acknowledging that its previous prediction of a weakening dollar had failed. The AI ​​boom has driven up US real interest rates, attracted massive equity inflows, reignited inflationary pressures, and prompted the Federal Reserve to adopt a hawkish stance, collectively shaping the current "AI dollar" landscape. The dollar is already more than 20% higher than its four-year average and ranks among the most expensive currencies in the G10 based on three fundamental valuation indicators. Deutsche Bank predicts that the US dollar will continue its strength in the first half of 2027, with a moderate decline in the second half, but will remain at a high level overall. The report also warns that the dollar's dependence on the AI ​​capital expenditure cycle is deepening, and if market expectations for AI returns are significantly lowered, the two main pillars supporting the dollar—US real interest rates and equity capital inflows—will collapse simultaneously, posing a substantial downside risk to the dollar. The AI ​​boom supports the "dollar exceptionalism" theory. The core driving force behind the dollar's strength originates from within the United States, and this trend may continue or even intensify in the short term. In recent months, US inflation has accelerated again, with the core PCE deflator expected to exceed 3%, pushing interest rate markets to repric and bringing the dollar back into the ranks of the top three highest-yielding currencies in the G10—a position it had previously relinquished by the end of 2025. Deutsche Bank data shows that historically, the dollar has rarely entered a downward cycle when offering high interest rates. US inflation has accelerated again in recent months, with the core PCE deflator expected to exceed 3%, driving interest rate repricing and pushing the dollar back into the top three highest-yielding currencies among the G10—a position it had previously relinquished by the end of 2025. Deutsche Bank data shows that historically, the dollar has rarely entered a downward cycle when offering high interest rates. The rise in real yields has simultaneously boosted expectations for the US neutral interest rate, which has increased by about 50 basis points this year, while the Eurozone has remained almost unchanged over the same period. Meanwhile, US GDP growth expectations have returned to the top of the G10, capital expenditure growth is about twice that of other economies, and the AI-driven capacity expansion cycle lays the foundation for productivity gains, providing a positive stimulus to the foreign exchange market. Meanwhile, US GDP growth is expected to return to the top of the G10, with capital expenditure growth roughly twice that of other economies. The AI-driven capacity expansion cycle lays the foundation for productivity gains, providing a positive stimulus to the foreign exchange market.

Equity inflows are dominant, while fixed-income funds show signs of diversion

In terms of capital flows, the US remains the core magnet for global equity investment. Foreign capital inflows into the US stock market have exceeded $1 trillion annually, becoming a major source of financing for the US external deficit. Moreover, such funds typically have a low hedging ratio, providing a more direct support for the US dollar. However, the flow of fixed-income funds is quietly changing. Data from Deutsche Bank shows that inflows into US bonds have slowed, while inflows into bonds in other G10 markets such as Canada and Japan have rebounded significantly, shaking the market narrative of "TINA" (No Other Choice). Foreign exchange reserve management institutions have also been continuously increasing their allocations to other smaller currencies over the past year and a half. This trend is worth noting—if the diversification value of dollar assets continues to decline, upward pressure on hedging ratios will increase accordingly. High valuations and twin deficits pose medium-term risks. The medium-term outlook for the US dollar faces multiple structural pressures. The most concerning is its over-reliance on the AI ​​capital expenditure cycle—related capital expenditures have increased nearly fivefold in the past three years, but the growth-driving effect of this momentum is expected to gradually diminish after 2028. The volatility in tech stocks has not yet transmitted to the dollar, but Deutsche Bank believes that once AI capital expenditure expectations are more significantly revised downwards, the dollar will face a substantial shock. Meanwhile, the US fiscal deficit has stabilized at approximately 6% of GDP, while the current account deficit is widening again, approaching 4% of GDP, nearing the worst level among G10 countries. From the perspective of trade-weighted real exchange rates, the potential trade deficit has shown a long-term trend of deterioration, only masked in the overall data due to the US energy balance turning positive. Tariff risks are also a concern—historical experience in recent years shows that tariff threats tend to depress the dollar rather than push it up.

Author: Paul Klay Source: X, @PaulKlayVC Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Over the past few years, the crypto market has seen a recurring array of different schemes. I believe these schemes are the key reason why it's almost impossible to make money in the crypto industry as easily as it used to be. And I don't think those opportunities will return.

...span>

Below I will discuss four of the biggest and most common tactics, which I believe played a decisive role in the process.

I. Trump and Insider Trading

Trump realized he had a huge opportunity to influence the crypto and stock markets and actively used it. Here we will only talk about crypto because it is much smaller, less stable, and easier to manipulate.

At this point, you possess a machine that appears to be able to print money infinitely.

When contract trading is open and you control most of the supply, you can observe how many people are shorting and how many are going long. You choose the side that is favorable to you, buy or sell a sufficient amount to trigger the liquidation of the opposing side, and then take the profits. Repeat this process as many times as possible until your token is delisted or the strategy becomes ineffective. To scale this strategy, you must have contracts listed on top exchanges because of the trading volume. Regardless of the actual quality of your project, as long as your token is listed on Binance contracts, it can attract hundreds of millions of dollars in trading volume.

III. Severely Inflated Valuations: Revenue Can't Support Them

Cryptoelectronics is still a relatively young industry, so projects often receive very high valuation multiples. Many people genuinely don't understand what they're being told. There are countless technologies, ambitious projects, etc., which is perfectly normal.

Like all other industries, most projects with flawed assumptions will eventually shut down; only a few projects drive the market forward.

However encryption has two key differences:

  • How is revenue generated

Due to the nature of the market—most people are there to make money easily, and due to the packaging of projects by many founders and marketers—the end result is that almost everyone's real motivation is to make money, not to solve problems.

Founders encourage users to use their technology by promising potential rewards through airdrops.

Returning to the basic principle of the market: as long as new people keep entering, this model can operate. But theoretically, without creating real value, it is simply impossible to sustain in the long run.

Everyone wants to make money, but someone has to lose money. So founders start mass-producing projects, using token issuance as a way to exit liquidity.

I know many teams used to launch several projects every week, and they still do. Think about it, there are several projects every week. They just need to package the projects, fabricate impressive data, pay KOLs to promote them, and then the profits come.

IV. Abusing Funds and Running Away

data.title: DeepSeek's funding list revealed: an all-star lineup of 31 investors.
data.description:
Money came in, but tickets didn't—this marks the first time the Chinese AI industry chain has collectively chosen sides.

—Written after the list of 31 companies surfaced

On November 17th, Hangzhou Deep Search Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd. completed a round of business registration changes. Its registered capital jumped from 16.4475 million yuan to 19.9187 million yuan, an increase of 21.1%. The new shareholder is a shareholding platform established just three months ago—Hangzhou Chengyan Enterprise Management Consulting Partnership.

What truly went viral in the investment community wasn't this number, but rather the additional layer above it: Hangzhou Chengyan's registered capital surged from 6,000 yuan to 3.439 billion yuan, with 31 new partners added at once.

A list that comprehensively covers almost the entire upstream and downstream of China's AI industry chain. I. First, let's solidify the figures. Note: Reports regarding amounts and valuations should be preceded by the statement—"Market estimates, not officially confirmed by DeepSeek." Under this premise, the mainstream narrative is as follows:
NumbersNumbersNumbers
105.5 billionThis round of fundraising
615.5 billionPost-investment valuation
51 billionFirst round of fundraising (June 2026)
≈400 billionFirst round post-investment valuation
Over 150 billionTotal funds raised in four months

— Qichacha Business Registration Change Records: Registered Capital and Shareholder Shares Change Simultaneously

Two rounds of financing totaling over 150 billion yuan within four months have broken the record for single-round financing in China's AI industry.

What can be confirmed from the business registration perspective is that Hangzhou Chengyan holds 17.265% of Deep Search's shares, making it the third-largest shareholder; the largest shareholder, Ningbo Cheng'en, holds 49.70%, and Liang Wenfeng personally holds 25.60% (a dilution of approximately 5.4 percentage points compared to before the change).

Beyond the numbers, what's more noteworthy is who's on the list and how they entered the picture.

II. The 31 companies are not scattered individuals, but rather five camps

The structure is very clear, arranged according to the investment ratio of Hangzhou Chengyan:

— Changes in Partner Investment: A Summary of the Investment Ratios of the 31 Institutions

Tier 1: Internet + New Energy Dual Core

Tencent's Shanghai Hengxiu holds 9.5653%, and CATL, through three funds—Xiamen Times Yiyuan, Times Shenyuan, and Fujian Times Zeyuan—holds a combined 9.5653%, making them the largest external investors. Working backward from 105.5 billion, each invests approximately 10 billion. Tencent's cumulative investment in the two rounds has reached 20 billion, while CATL's investment has increased from 5 billion in the first round to 10 billion in this round.

Second Tier: State-Owned Enterprises + Securities Firms

China Mobile Investment Holding and CITIC Securities Investment each hold 7.6522%; China Life's equity-related entities hold 4.78%; China Telecom holds 2.87%; CICC Hebei Steel and CICC Pucheng are also included. According to the Shanghai Securities News, at least nine securities firms have indirectly entered the market, investing a total of approximately 9.52 billion yuan. In the first round, state-owned capital accounted for only about 2%, but this round it jumped directly to about 27%.

Third Tier: Terminals and Manufacturing

vivo 2.87%, Midea 2.87%, Luxshare Precision (Lizhen Precision) 2.77%, GigaDevice 1.43%, Geely Investment 0.96%, SMIC Capital 1.60%, and Hangzhou Shixi GigaDevice No. 1 (related to Shixi Capital) 3.35%. Mobile phones, home appliances, automobile manufacturing, storage, wafer equipment—basically all the hardware companies that could participate are involved.

Tier 4: Internet Scenarios

Meituan Longzhu 2.87%, NetEase Leihuo Wanxiang 2.39%, Ctrip-affiliated Shanghai Kehui 1.43%, Xiaohongshu (Xingyin Information) 0.96%. These four names answer the same question—where to place the model after training.

Tier 5: Familiar Faces in the Primary Market

Lisi 7.17%, Boyu 3.35%, CPE Yuanfeng 3.35%, Zhengxin Valley 3.35%, Shixiang 3.35%, IDG 3.32%, Gaorong 2.87%, Junlian 2.87%, Hongzhuo 1.43%, Hengdian Capital 1.43%. Among them, Lisi, IDG, Zhengxin Valley, and Shixiang participated in the first round and received priority allocations in this round.

CampRepresentative Investors
Internet + New EnergyTencent, CATL
National Team + Securities FirmsChina Mobile, CITIC Securities, China Life Insurance, 9 securities firms
Terminals and Manufacturingvivo, Midea, Luxshare, Geely, SMIC
Internet ScenariosMeituan, NetEase, Ctrip, Xiaohongshu
Familiar Faces in the Primary MarketLisi, IDG, Zhenxin Valley, Shixiang

Upstream chips, midstream computing power, downstream scenarios, with state-owned enterprises standing alongside.

III. More crucial than "who invested" is "how they invested."

None of the 31 external shareholders appear directly on Deep Search's shareholder list.

All shares are indirectly held through Hangzhou Chengyan, whose general partner (GP) is Hangzhou Chengce Business Consulting Co., Ltd.—Liang Wenfeng holds 99% of the shares in this company. Liang Wenfeng himself even withdrew from the list of direct partners of Hangzhou Chengyan, retaining only control as a GP.

— Liang Wenfeng: Money Came In, Control Remained Unchanged "In other words: Money came in, but votes didn't." The 31 companies are limited partners (LPs), enjoying financial returns but not voting rights or board seats. Securities Times estimates that after this round of capital increase, Liang Wenfeng's direct and indirect shareholding remains approximately 67.42%, meaning the entry of hundreds of billions of yuan in capital has not shaken his control in the slightest. In today's financing market, such a stance is extremely rare. According to feedback from investors contacted by the Daily Economic News, institutions seeking more flexibility in terms of terms are generally met with the response of "no room for negotiation." In the past, investors chose projects; this round, projects choose investors—they must pass thorough due diligence, accept long lock-up periods, and relinquish governance rights to qualify for entry. The only exception: The National Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund directly invested in Deepin's Ontology, holding 0.39% of the shares. IV. What is this list betting on? If we rearrange the 31 companies according to their "purpose," the logic becomes clear: Computing power and energy CATL, SMIC, GigaDevice, Stony Brook—the next bottleneck for large-scale models is not algorithms, but electricity and chips.

Cloud and Government/Enterprise Channel

China Mobile, China Telecom, and China Life—determine how many government and enterprise data centers the model can be placed in.

Terminal Entry Point

vivo, Midea, Luxshare, and Geely—for the model to grow a body, it must first be placed in mobile phones, home appliances, and automobiles.

Scenario Traffic

Tencent, Meituan, Xiaohongshu, NetEase, and Ctrip—daily active users are the real consumers of inference computing power.

Capitalization Channel

CITIC Securities, CICC Group, and at least 7 other securities firms—pre-IPO resource preparation.

Industrial capital accounts for over 50% of the investment, making it the absolute main force in this round.

It's not money looking for models, it's the industry chain looking for hubs.

This is completely different from the financing structure of the "financial capital chasing trends" wave of 2023-2024—this time it's not money looking for models, but the industry chain looking for hubs. "DeepSeek has been regarded by the market as a hub driving the operation of domestic computing power, energy, and application ecosystems." The list of 31 companies is a concrete manifestation of this judgment. V. The Step That Hasn't Been Fulfilled Yet Business registration ≠ official financing announcement, and official financing announcement ≠ listing. Currently, the only confirmed fact is that CITIC Securities has entered the market to prepare for listing, but the formal guidance agreement and the filing with the Zhejiang Securities Regulatory Bureau have not yet been completed. The "trillion-yuan market value" and "Hangzhou's second trillion-yuan listed company" circulating in the market are expectations extrapolated by institutions based on a valuation of 615.5 billion yuan, not the actual price.

Tip: Three things really need to be observed:

  1. When will the official figures of 105.5 billion / 615.5 billion be confirmed? Currently, it's all based on reverse engineering.
  2. Computing power procurement pace—the bulk of the 150 billion is invested in computing power; the supplier list will reveal more about the strategic direction than the shareholder list.
  3. Can the GP/LP structure pass the STAR Market review?—Highly concentrated control + 31 non-voting LPs is the most important part to explain in the prospectus.

For the first time, the Chinese AI industry chain has collectively chosen sides.

The value of this list of 31 people lies not in "how much money was raised," but in "who is willing to hand over their money without taking a vote."

When Tencent, CATL, China Mobile, CITIC, Meituan, Geely, Midea, and Vivo are all willing to squeeze into a shell controlled by a single founder, and still feel there aren't enough spots— "The market's vote with real money is more honest than any valuation figure." As for trillions of dollars, as for IPOs, that's for the next chapter. Today's chapter title is already written: China's AI Industry Chain, for the First Time, Collectively Takes Sides.

data.title: Behind the 9.13% decrease in mining difficulty: Texas electricity prices are the main reason.
data.description:
On November 14th, Bitcoin mining difficulty decreased by 9.13%, marking the largest drop since June. The market's initial reaction is often to attribute this to Bitcoin's price, but the data points to electricity prices in West Texas. Electricity costs exceed mining revenue. Mining rigs are only economically viable when mining revenue exceeds electricity costs. Energy hashrate is a metric used to measure this profitability; it reflects the mining revenue a rig can generate per megawatt-hour (MWh) of electricity consumed, and can be understood as the break-even electricity price for mining rigs. Taking a mining rig with an energy efficiency ratio of 25J/TH as an example, during the difficulty adjustment period from October 29th to November 14th, its average break-even electricity price was $54/MWh. However, electricity prices in West Texas surged and exceeded this threshold. From November 7th to 11th, the average daily electricity price reached $64 to $122/MWh. The sharp drop in wind power generation was the main reason: wind power output in West Texas plummeted from 12.6 gigawatts (GW) on November 4th to approximately 1 GW from November 7th to 9th, pushing the 345 kV transmission lines to their maximum capacity. This resulted in West Texas's electricity price being $47/MWh higher than other parts of the state on November 9th. The situation was worst in the evening: after sunset and the disappearance of solar power generation, the average electricity price from 5 pm to 11 pm reached $80 to $98/MWh. On November 11, the power shortage spread throughout the state, with wind power dropping to 2 to 4 gigawatts after sunset, and by around 9 pm, electricity prices in the north, south, and west regions soaring to $500 to $650/MWh. Comparison of Daily Real-Time Electricity Prices and 25J/TH Energy Hashrate Prices in ERCOT West From October 29 to November 14, West Texas experienced 45% of the time when electricity prices exceeded the mining revenue of 25J/TH energy efficiency ratio mining rigs (i.e., in a loss-making state), far higher than the 9% during the period from October 16 to 29. This percentage of loss-making periods is the highest in at least a year, and its duration even exceeds the level during the winter storm in late January of this year.

Percentage of Loss-Making Mining Periods in Western ERCOT During Difficulty Cycles from November 2025 to November 2026

Electricity Price (Not Cryptocurrency Price) Determines Hashrate Price

Since hashrate prices also declined during the same period, we conducted a separate analysis of electricity price and hashrate price. Data shows that the percentage of time local miners were operating at a loss jumped from 9% to 45%, a surge of 36 percentage points.

As hashrate prices also declined during the same period, we conducted a separate analysis of electricity price and hashrate price. Data shows that the percentage of time local miners were operating at a loss jumped from 9% to 45%, a surge of 36 percentage points.

Estimated Bitcoin Network Hashrate

Next Step

Mining machines shut down due to high electricity prices will quickly restart once electricity prices drop. Since the last difficulty adjustment, the average block time across the network has shortened to 9.1 minutes. Based on this speed, even if the price of Bitcoin continues to decline, the mining difficulty will still increase significantly by about 10% in the next cycle adjustment. At that time, the hashrate price will be compressed from $30 to $27; and for mainstream 25J/TH energy efficiency mining machines, the break-even electricity price (energy hashrate cost line) will also drop to $45/MWh. However, only 538 of the 2,016 blocks in this cycle have been completed so far, and it is too early to draw conclusions—just on Monday afternoon (November 16), the electricity price in West Texas broke through the $120/MWh mark again. Looking ahead, Luxor's hashrate forward market pricing shows that the average hashrate price for the next six months will be $28.23, or 0.000437 BTC/PH/s/day. Miners can now lock in this revenue level in advance; while buyers can also use this opportunity to lock in their computing power procurement costs at the same level up to May 2027. data.title: Satoshi Nakamoto's dormant forum resurfaces: Administrator account was still logged in in 2014.
data.description:
Written by: Luis Blanco, beincrypto; Translated by: Saoirse, Foresight News

Not long after the 18th anniversary of the release of the Bitcoin white paper, this long-dormant forum built by Satoshi Nakamoto has resurfaced. A related post on the X platform has sparked heated discussions within the community. The forum administrator account was still logged in in 2014, a detail that adds further complexity to the mystery of the identity of Satoshi Nakamoto, the anonymous founder of Bitcoin.

Snapshot information shows that the forum had only three members, all of whom held administrator privileges. The account "satoshi" (Nakamoto Satoshi) was registered on November 13, 2009, posted a total of 5 posts, and was last active on November 21, 2009. The account "sirius-m" was registered on November 15, but never posted. The third account, "admin," was registered on November 14, 2009. Intriguingly, this account was last logged in on June 17, 2014.

Who logged into this forum in 2014?

Murray found a crucial clue: an email sent by Satoshi Nakamoto to Martti Malmi, an early Bitcoin developer, on November 14, 2009. In the email, Nakamoto mentioned that InvisionFree was migrating to ZetaBoards, so he created this forum and sent the administrator account's login credentials and password to Martti Malmi. The timeline matches perfectly: the email was sent on the same day the admin account was registered, and sirius-m was an ID Martti Malmi had used for a long time. However, the difficulty lies in the fact that at least two people possessed this administrator password. Therefore, it remains impossible to confirm who logged into the account in 2014. Satoshi Nakamoto shared the administrator login information for the ZetaBoards forum with Martti Malmi in an email dated November 14, 2009. Source: mmalmi.github.io. This uncertainty adds another layer to the already perplexing mystery of Satoshi Nakamoto's identity. Eighteen years after the white paper was released, Satoshi Nakamoto's true identity remains unresolved. Over the years, many candidates have been speculated to be cypherpunks, including Hal Finney, Nick Szabo, and Adam Back. In 2024, the HBO documentary *Money Electric* pointed the finger at developer Peter Todd, but Todd denied it. That same year, a British court ruled that Craig Wright was not Satoshi Nakamoto. Recently, a new claim has emerged. Early Bitcoin practitioner Charlie Shrem claims that researchers are tracking Satoshi Nakamoto's whereabouts using multiple aliases. According to Shrem, Nakamoto never left the crypto community; he simply continued to speak within it under different aliases. However, this research team does not intend to disclose Nakamoto's identity.

data.title: China's AI Migration
data.description:
Text｜Sleepy

There is a pattern in industrial history: the closer we get to a new generation, the clearer it becomes where a technology truly originated.

In England during the 1760s and 1770s, water-powered spinning machines had just been invented. Factory owners headed north to find valleys in Derbyshire and Lancashire on either side of the Pennine Mountains. At that time, Watt's steam engine had not yet entered textile factories; water turbines were still used to power the spindles. A few decades later, steam engines became widespread, and factories gradually moved from valleys to coalfields and the outskirts of cities.

Every technological advancement begins with the invention of an algorithm, a blueprint, or a machine, followed by a massive geographical relocation involving the search for electricity, water, and land. When times are calm, the global supply chain resembles a smooth net, and computing power can be mobilized even across the Pacific Ocean. This easily creates the illusion that software and intelligence are weightless and undemanding. However, once blockades and restrictions are encountered, the cloud returns to the ground, revealing its true nature as heavy industry: it requires electricity, is sensitive to heat, is particular about power lines, and, most importantly, depends on the manufacturer of the chips housed in those rows of server racks. On October 16, 1964, at Lop Nur, China successfully detonated its first atomic bomb, codenamed "596". Five years earlier, on June 20, 1959, the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union sent a letter to the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, deciding to temporarily suspend the provision of the atomic bomb teaching models and blueprints agreed upon in the agreement.

Mushroom cloud from the explosion of China's first atomic bomb in Lop Nur in 1964 | Image source: People's Pictorial

Almost in the same autumn, the site selection policy for the Third Front construction was set: near mountains, dispersed, and concealed. In practice, two more words were added: underground. Over the next decade, millions of workers, cadres, intellectuals, and PLA soldiers left the cities of the east and northeast, moving machine tools, blast furnaces, and laboratories into the mountains of the southwest and northwest. At its peak, more than 4 million people were involved. More than half a century has passed, and the world's most cutting-edge industries have been replaced by large-scale models. Those training these large models have a daily routine: saving checkpoints. Thousands or even tens of thousands of accelerator cards run continuously for months; if even one card disconnects, training is interrupted. Every so often, all the model's weights, optimizer states, and random number seeds are saved so that if a problem occurs, training can resume from the most recent node. This word also has a literal meaning in English: border checkpoint. In November 2026, after a long search across the equator, China's large model industry finally reached its checkpoint. The story begins with four suitcases bound for Kuala Lumpur. In early March 2025, four Chinese engineers flew from Beijing to Malaysia. Each of them carried a suitcase containing 15 hard drives, totaling 80TB of data. Their destination was a data center in Malaysia, where their employer had rented approximately 300 servers equipped with advanced NVIDIA chips. For this flight, their colleagues back home began refining the dataset and repeatedly debugging the training program more than eight weeks in advance. Once the data is packed into boxes and leaves the country, it's difficult to start over as easily as it would be back home in a foreign server room. The reason for not transferring it over the network was that network transmission "might take several months," making physical transfer faster. According to the plan, what they ultimately wanted to bring back was much smaller, only a few hundred gigabytes—the trained model parameters. This is the most basic aspect of the first large-scale computing power migration in China; if the data can't get in, it has to be shipped out. What forced the engineers to take to the airport was the increasingly stringent chip ban over the past few years. On October 7, 2022, the US banned the sale of Nvidia A100 and H100 chips to China for the first time; Nvidia quickly modified the A800 and H800 specifically for the Chinese market, reducing interconnect bandwidth. Just one year later, on October 17, 2023, even the slower versions were shut out.

2022 and 2023 US Advanced Computing Chip Export Control Rules | Image Source: Government Website

That year, domestic market demand for advanced computing chips was extremely high. The price of the A100 jumped from around 40,000 yuan at the beginning of the year to nearly 250,000 yuan; in the week after the new regulations were implemented in October, the price of the H800 almost doubled, with a complete 8-card system being quoted as 2.45 million yuan by distributors.

At the same time, domestic computing infrastructure experienced a premature development. Between 2023 and 2024, more than 500 intelligent computing center projects were announced across various regions, with at least 150 already operational by the end of 2024. On one hand, labs were struggling to purchase GPUs despite having cash, while on the other hand, server rooms across the country were vacant. This was due to the physical barriers to training large-scale models. Cutting-edge models require tens of thousands of high-end GPUs of the same generation connected to a large cluster via a high-speed network. However, the server rooms scattered across the country mostly contained fragmented, outdated, and poorly connected inference cards or older-generation graphics cards. Fortunately, at the time, US export controls had a loophole, allowing only buying and selling, not leasing. Companies headquartered in China couldn't import chips into the country, but they could rent data centers from overseas cloud providers and non-Chinese owners. The industry quickly devised a division of labor: pre-training, which demands the most computing power and requires the highest cluster communication bandwidth, was done in overseas data centers; once the model was trained, the weights were brought back to China, where domestic computing power pools handled daily user inference. Once this approach worked, the rudimentary method of carrying suitcases was quickly replaced by modern cloud infrastructure. Later, engineers no longer needed to travel abroad. The core clause of the new regulations is only one: any data center in the world that provides more than 12 million TPPs of computing power to a company headquartered in China (including its overseas subsidiaries) must obtain a license from the US Department of Commerce in advance to transport advanced chips to that data center. 12 million TPPs, when converted, is roughly equivalent to 750 H100 chips, or about four or five server racks. Training a cutting-edge model with trillions of parameters requires thousands or even tens of thousands of cards. Four or five server racks wouldn't even be enough. For existing overseas data centers already serving Chinese customers, the new regulations provide a 90-day grace period to apply for licenses; otherwise, they "will face future export restrictions." Starting from November 19th, the 90-day deadline falls around February 17th, 2027. The new regulations include a presumption clause: if an overseas data center refuses to provide, or is unable to provide, customer due diligence information, this act itself will be considered a "red flag," and the exporter can be "presumed" to be "aware." In other words, if you can't say whose code is running in the data center, it's assumed you're problematic. Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil are specifically named; shipments of advanced AI chips to these five countries require permits and approvals. If the buyer is a company headquartered in the United States, the exporter can be exempted by submitting monthly reports. Physical supply disruptions follow closely behind.
